directions: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Reka is an early-to-midseason highbush blueberry bred in New Zealand, valued for its compact, vigorous, upright bush and large, firm berries with a bright, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that ripens ahead of many standard highbush varieties. The early ripening window makes it useful for extending the front end of a home blueberry harvest when paired with midseason and late varieties. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out the oldest canes each winter to maintain vigor, and plant alongside a second highbush variety to improve pollination and overall yield.

Toro was bred at Rutgers University and released for its exceptionally large, firm, sweet, light-blue berries carried on a vigorous, upright, well-branched bush that stands up well to mechanical harvesting as well as home picking, with good resistance to several common blueberry diseases. Ripening in midseason, it produces heavy, concentrated crops that hold well on the bush without softening quickly, giving a wider picking window than some earlier varieties. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out the oldest canes each winter, and plant alongside a second highbush variety to improve pollination and overall yield.

Bluejay was bred at Michigan State University for reliable cold hardiness and good resistance to several diseases that affect blueberries in humid climates, including some tolerance of mummy berry, producing firm, light-blue, mildly sweet berries in early to midseason on a vigorous, upright bush. The bush's tolerance for cold and its dependable, consistent production have made it a long-standing favorite for northern home orchards and commercial plantings alike, even as newer releases have entered the market. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out the oldest canes each winter to maintain vigor, and plant alongside a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield.

Elliott is prized above all for ripening later than almost any other highbush blueberry, extending the home harvest well into fall after earlier varieties have finished, with firm, small to medium, light-blue berries that start out fairly tart and develop better sweetness the longer they are left to fully color on the bush. The very late ripening window also means the crop largely escapes the peak pressure of many early-season pests and diseases. The vigorous, upright bush stores its fruit well both on the plant and after picking, making Elliott a valuable addition alongside early- and midseason varieties for gardeners wanting the longest possible blueberry season. Give full sun and consistent moisture, prune out old canes each winter, and plant with a second highbush variety for best pollination.

planting.note: Set out bare-root or potted bushes in early spring once soil is workable, into strongly acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or pine bark; Northland is exceptionally cold-hardy and well suited to zone 3-7 winters.

directions: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Northland was bred at Michigan State University by crossing highbush and lowbush blueberry species, resulting in a compact, spreading 'half-high' bush notable for extreme cold hardiness that lets it survive winters too harsh for standard highbush varieties. The medium-sized berries have good, classic sweet blueberry flavor and ripen reliably even in short northern growing seasons, and the naturally lower, denser habit makes the bush useful as an informal hedge or foundation planting in addition to its fruiting value. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune lightly each winter to remove the oldest wood, and plant with a second variety to improve pollination and yield.
